Use a before consonant sounds (a cat, a university /ju/). Use an before vowel sounds (an apple, an hour). Sound matters, not only spelling.
the marks something specific or already known (the sun, the book I mentioned). Skip articles for most proper names and general plurals (Dogs bark).
No article for general plural/mass nouns (Water is wet; Cars need fuel) and most names (London, Sarah) unless specified.
Present of be: I am, you/we/they are, he/she/it is. Negatives: am not, are not (aren't), is not (isn't).
Past of be: I/he/she/it was; you/we/they were. Negatives: was not (wasn't), were not (weren't).
Present have: I/you/we/they have; he/she/it has. Past: had for all. Possessive spoken form: I've got / she's got (informal).
Questions/negatives in present simple use do/does: Do you work? Does she work? Past: did for all (Did they go?).
Present simple: base verb; he/she/it adds -s/-es (she works). Use for habits, facts, schedules. Negative: do/does not + base.
Present continuous: am/is/are + -ing (I am reading). Use for now/temporary actions. Spelling: run→running, make→making.
Past simple: regular verbs add -ed (walked). Irregulars change form (go→went). Negative: did not + base (did not go).
will + base for decisions/promises/predictions (I will help). am/is/are going to + base for plans/evidence-based future.
have/has + past participle (I have seen; she has gone). Links past to now: experience, unfinished time, result now.
go → went → gone. Present: go/goes. Past simple: went. Perfect: have/has gone.
see → saw → seen.
eat → ate → eaten.
write → wrote → written.
come → came → come (past participle same as base).
take → took → taken.
give → gave → given.
get → got → got (US often gotten as participle).
make → made → made.
know → knew → known.
think → thought → thought.
say → said → said.
tell → told → told. tell someone something; say something (to someone).
A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea (teacher, city, book, freedom). Count nouns can be plural; mass nouns usually are not (water, advice).
A verb shows action or state (run, think, is, have). It carries tense and agreement with the subject.
An adjective describes a noun (a red car, a happy child). Order often: opinion-size-age-color-noun.
An adverb modifies a verb, adjective, or adverb (run quickly, very tall, quite slowly). Many end in -ly but not all (fast, well, often).
Subject: I you he she it we they. Object: me you him her it us them. Possessive adj: my your his her its our their.
Singular subject → singular verb (He works). Plural → plural (They work). Note: I/you take base without -s (I work, you work).
Yes/no: auxiliary + subject + base (Do you like tea? Is she ready?). Wh-: wh-word + auxiliary + subject + base (Where do you live?).
Add not after auxiliary/modal (is not, cannot, will not) or use do/does/did + not + base in simple tenses (does not know).
Most nouns +s (cats). -s/-x/-ch/-sh → -es (boxes, watches). consonant+y → -ies (city→cities). Irregular: child→children, mouse→mice, person→people.
Short adj: -er/-est (taller, tallest). Long: more/most (more useful). Irregular: good→better→best; bad→worse→worst.
hello/hi (greeting); goodbye/bye (leaving); please (polite request); thank you/thanks (gratitude); you're welcome (reply to thanks).
1 one, 2 two, 3 three, 4 four, 5 five, 6 six, 7 seven, 8 eight, 9 nine, 10 ten.
Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday. Weekend = Saturday + Sunday.
red, blue, green, yellow, black, white, orange, purple, brown, gray/grey, pink.
mother/mom, father/dad, parent(s), sister, brother, sibling, son, daughter, child/children, grandmother, grandfather.
What time is it? It's three o'clock; half past three (3:30); quarter past (3:15); quarter to four (3:45). a.m./p.m. for 12-hour clock.
bread, water, milk, rice, meat, fish, fruit, vegetable, apple, egg, cheese, coffee, tea. meal: breakfast, lunch, dinner.
in = inside/enclosed (in a room, in London). on = surface/street line (on the table, on Main Street). at = point (at the door, at school as institution).
at + clock time (at 5). on + day/date (on Monday, on May 1). in + month/year/period (in July, in 2026, in the morning).
can = ability/permission; could = past ability or polite. must = strong necessity; should = advice. Modal + base verb (no to): can go, must leave.
there is + singular/mass (there is a book; there is water). there are + plural (there are books). Past: there was / there were.
Countable: a/an, many, few, number (apples). Uncountable: much, little, some (water, information, rice) — no a/an, no plural -s usually.
this/these = near (this book, these books). that/those = farther (that car, those cars).
Default: Subject–Verb–Object (She reads books). Adjectives before nouns (a blue sky). Time often last (I saw him yesterday).
Capitalize sentence starts, the pronoun I, names, days, months, nationalities, languages (English), places. Not mid-sentence common nouns.
Period . ends statements. Question mark ? ends questions. Comma , separates lists and clauses. Apostrophe ' for possession (Sam's) and contractions (don't).
